subject: General Knowledge
topic: Famous battles of India — mixed tiers

questions.stem: The Battle of Plassey (1757), which gave the British East India Company decisive control over Bengal, was fought on the banks of which river?

options.option_text: Damodar River, flowing through Burdwan district
Bhagirathi River, a distributary of the Ganges
Teesta River, flowing through Jalpaiguri district
Rupnarayan River, near the Bengal delta region

questions.explanation: B is correct. The battlefield at Palashi (Plassey) in Nadia district, West Bengal, lies on the banks of the Bhagirathi River (a Ganges distributary), about 150 km north of Kolkata near Murshidabad. Option A is wrong: the Damodar flows further south through Burdwan and was entirely unrelated to the battle. Option C (Teesta) is in far-north Bengal near Siliguri, hundreds of kilometres from Plassey.

questions.stem: Babur's victory at the First Battle of Panipat (1526) owed much to a mobile flanking manoeuvre combined with artillery fire that was new to northern India. What was this combined tactic called?

options.option_text: Tulugma — outflanking with mobile cavalry and artillery fire
Ghulam — elite slave-soldier shock corps deployed at the centre
Mandala — concentric ring formation traditionally used by Rajputs
Chappa — surprise night-raid tactic directed against Ibrahim Lodi

questions.explanation: A is correct. Babur employed the Tulugma tactic: flanking cavalry wings wheeled inward to encircle Ibrahim Lodi's larger force while matchlocks and field guns at the centre caused panic among war elephants. This combination of firearms and mobile envelopment was decisive. Option C (Mandala) is a Rajput-era formation concept, not a Mughal tactic, and was not used here. Option D (Chappa) is not a recognised Timurid or Mughal tactical term.

questions.stem: The Battle of Buxar (1764) is considered historically more decisive than Plassey because it was fought against a three-power coalition. Which option correctly identifies all three allied powers?

options.option_text: Mir Qasim (Bengal), Hyder Ali (Mysore), Nizam Ali Khan (Hyderabad)
Mir Qasim (Bengal), Shah Alam II (Mughal), Shuja-ud-Daulah (Awadh)
Shuja-ud-Daulah (Awadh), Maratha Confederacy, and the Sikh Misl forces
Mir Jafar (Bengal), Tipu Sultan (Mysore), and Haider Ali (Carnatic)

questions.explanation: B is correct. The three allies at Buxar were Mir Qasim (deposed Nawab of Bengal), Shah Alam II (Mughal Emperor), and Shuja-ud-Daulah (Nawab of Awadh). Option A is a strong trap — Hyder Ali and the Nizam were real British adversaries but fought separately in the Deccan; they were not at Buxar. Option D is wrong: Mir Jafar was a British collaborator, not an opponent, and Tipu Sultan was only a child in 1764 and not yet a political figure.

questions.stem: The Battle of Talikota (1565), which effectively ended the Vijayanagara Empire, is also known by the name of two nearby villages where the actual fighting took place. What is that alternate name?

options.option_text: Battle of Rakshasi-Tangadi, named after two adjoining villages
Battle of Bijapur, named after the dominant sultanate in the alliance
Battle of Krishnagiri, named after a nearby fortified hilltop location
Battle of Raichur, since Vijayanagara lost the Raichur Doab here

questions.explanation: A is correct. The engagement is also called the Battle of Rakshasi-Tangadi after the two villages (Raksasa and Tangadagi) near the actual site in present-day Karnataka. Option B is wrong: Bijapur was one member of the four-sultanate confederacy (Bijapur, Bidar, Ahmadnagar, Golconda) but the battle was not fought there. Option D is a plausible trap: Raichur Doab was contested in the separate Battle of Raichur (1520) between Vijayanagara and Bijapur — a different event entirely.

questions.stem: Akbar did not personally lead his forces at the Battle of Haldighati (1576) against Maharana Pratap. Who was appointed to command the Mughal imperial army for this engagement?

options.option_text: Todar Mal, Akbar's revenue minister who also led military campaigns
Man Singh I of Amber, a Rajput commander in the Mughal imperial service
Prince Murad, Akbar's son deputed to lead the Rajputana campaign
Birbal, one of the Navaratnas who led Akbar's elite cavalry division

questions.explanation: B is correct. Man Singh I of Amber (Kachwaha Rajput, Akbar's brother-in-law and trusted general) commanded the Mughal forces at Haldighati. Option A is a tempting trap — Todar Mal did lead military operations, but he was engaged in the Bengal campaigns at this time and did not command at Haldighati. Option D is wrong: Birbal held no military command; he was a courtier and poet who died in the 1586 Yusufzai expedition, a separate event.

questions.stem: The Treaty of Allahabad (1765), signed after the Battle of Buxar, included a landmark agreement with Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II. Which provision most decisively transformed the East India Company from a trading firm into a territorial revenue power?

options.option_text: Grant of Diwani rights over Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa to the EIC
Payment of an annual tribute of ₹26 lakh by EIC to the Mughal Emperor
Transfer of Kora and Allahabad districts permanently to Shah Alam II
Right of free trade with Dastak passes across all Mughal territories

questions.explanation: A is correct. The Diwani grant — right to collect land revenue from Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa — made the EIC financially self-sustaining and sovereign in substance even while nominally acting as a Mughal agent. Option B is the sharpest trap: EIC did agree to pay ₹26 lakh annually to Shah Alam II, but this was a concession FROM EIC, not a power gain; the Diwani was the transformative acquisition. Option C (Kora and Allahabad) was land given TO Shah Alam II, also not a British gain.

questions.stem: The Third Battle of Panipat (1761) ended Maratha dominance in northern India. Who held actual supreme command of the Maratha forces and was killed during the engagement?

options.option_text: Vishwasrao, the teenage son of Peshwa Balaji Baji Rao with nominal command
Malharrao Holkar, the veteran Maratha cavalry general commanding the flanks
Sadashivrao Bhau, the Peshwa's cousin who held actual supreme command
Raghunathrao (Raghoba), who earlier led northern campaigns up to Attock

questions.explanation: C is correct. Sadashivrao Bhau (the Peshwa's cousin) was the actual commander-in-chief and was killed in the battle. Option A is the strongest trap: Vishwasrao (the Peshwa's son) held nominal titular command and was also killed early in the fighting, leading many students to confuse him as the 'supreme' commander. Option B is factually wrong in a key detail: Malharrao Holkar survived — he disengaged with his cavalry early, a controversial act still debated by historians. Option D is wrong: Raghunathrao led the 1758 Attock campaign but did not command at the 1761 battle.
